passage_title: The Night of the Pear Tree
passage:
Passage A

[1] The storm that took down the pear tree came on a Thursday in late August, the summer I was thirteen, and my parents were on the wrong side of it. They had driven into town that afternoon to sit with my grandmother, and by seven the creek road was under water. My father telephoned at nine. He said to put my brother in the hallway, away from the windows, and to save the flashlight for when we needed it, and then the line made a sound like frying and went dead.

[2] I did what he said. I dragged Teddy's mattress into the hall and lay down beside him, and because I had read that you could tell how far off lightning was by counting, I counted in my head between each flash and its thunder. Eleven. Then seven. Then four. Teddy was eight, and he asked me once whether we were going to die. I told him in my most bored voice that houses were built for this, and I sang him the only song I knew all the way through, a jingle for a tire store on the radio. He was asleep before ten. I remember being almost offended by how easily he went.

[3] The count reached nothing a little after midnight. The flash and the crack came together, and then a second noise, longer and lower, that seemed to run along underneath the floor. I sat up with the flashlight in my lap and did not turn it on. I did not wake him. There seemed no point in two of us being awake for it.

[4] At seven Teddy walked out into the yard in his pajamas, looked at the pear tree lying across the crushed roof of the shed, and said, "When did that happen?" I have told that line at every family dinner for thirty years. In our family it is the proof that my brother could sleep through the end of the world, and he has always laughed at it with everyone else.

[5] I tell it as a joke, but I know what it is to me. That was the night I stopped being the one who was looked after. Nobody handed me the job. It was simply lying there in the hallway, and I picked it up.

Passage B

[1] My sister tells the story of the pear tree every Thanksgiving, and she tells it well. She does my voice for the last line, higher than my voice ever was, and everyone laughs, and I laugh too, because it is a good story and it is mostly true. The part that is not true is the part about my being asleep.

[2] I was awake for all of it. Early on I asked her whether we were going to die, and she answered in a voice I had never heard from her, flat and slow, as if the question bored her. I was eight, but I knew that voice. It was the one our mother used on the telephone with the hospital. I understood that my being awake was one more thing my sister had to hold up, and that if I slept she would only have herself to hold. So I made my breathing go long and even, the way our father breathed in his chair after supper, and I kept it that way for three hours.

[3] She thinks she counted in her head. She counted in a whisper, eleven and seven and four, each number smaller than the last, and I lay there doing the arithmetic with her. She sang the tire jingle twice, not once; the second time, I think, was for herself. When the big noise came I was certain it was the house splitting along its middle, and keeping my eyes shut was the hardest thing I had ever done.

[4] The question in the morning was a real question, only not the one she hears. I knew when. I had been awake for it. What I did not know, until I stood in the wet grass, was what: that it had been the tree and not the house. The relief came out as the only sentence I could find.

[5] I have never corrected her, and I do not intend to. It is her story about the night she became the older one, and that part of it is true.

choices: her father had told her on the telephone to keep him away from the windows.
she had read that a hallway was the safest place in a house during lightning.
the bedroom ceiling had begun to leak once the creek road was under water.
her brother had asked to sleep somewhere he could hear her counting.
correct_answer: her father had told her on the telephone to keep him away from the windows.
explanation: Passage A says her father telephoned at nine and "said to put my brother in the hallway, away from the windows," and then "I did what he said. I dragged Teddy's mattress into the hall." What she had read about was counting the seconds between lightning and thunder, not where in a house to shelter. No leak is mentioned anywhere, and the creek road matters only because it kept her parents in town. Her brother asks her one thing, whether they are going to die; he never asks to hear her count.

passage:
Passage A

[1] The storm that took down the pear tree came on a Thursday in late August, the summer I was thirteen, and my parents were on the wrong side of it. They had driven into town that afternoon to sit with my grandmother, and by seven the creek road was under water. My father telephoned at nine. Eleven. Then seven. Then four. Teddy was eight, and he asked me once whether we were going to die. I told him in my most bored voice that houses were built for this, and I sang him the only song I knew all the way through, a jingle for a tire store on the radio. He was asleep before ten. passage_title: The Language on the Playground
passage:
[1] A language rarely dies the way a person does, on a single date. It goes quiet in stages. First it leaves the government offices and the schools, then the shops and the newspapers, and last of all the kitchen, at the moment when parents who still speak it to each other begin, for reasons that seem kind at the time, to speak something else to their children. Linguists call this a break in intergenerational transmission, and most regard it as the turning point. A language that infants are still learning at home can survive a great deal of neglect elsewhere; one that infants are no longer learning has, in effect, been given a date.

[2] That is why the most influential revival efforts of the last half century have aimed at the very young. In New Zealand in the early 1980s, Māori communities began opening kōhanga reo, or "language nests": preschools in which older native speakers looked after small children entirely in Māori. Hawaiian families followed within a few years with the Pūnana Leo preschools, built on the same idea. Their task was steeper. A law passed in 1896 had made English the sole medium of instruction in Hawaii's schools, and over the following generations the language retreated from public life and then from most homes. By the early 1980s, by most estimates, fewer than fifty children spoke it as a first language.

[3] In the sense that matters most to linguists, the nests worked: they produced children who could speak. Immersion programs grew upward behind them, grade by grade, until in both places a student could be taught in the language through the end of secondary school. There are now young adults in each country who spoke their heritage language before they could read English.

[4] Success, however, exposed a difficulty that few had planned for. Children who acquire a language mainly in classrooms often speak a version noticeably different from that of the elders who taught them, simpler in parts of its grammar, crowded with words coined for things the elders never needed to name, and shaped in its sounds by English. Some elders have said they find the young people's speech hard to follow, and some young speakers say they hesitate to use the language in front of elders for fear of being corrected. Researchers in several countries now study this group, often called "new speakers," and the tension between them and older native speakers turns up in revival movements almost everywhere.

[5] The worry about purity deserves a hearing. An elder who hears her language returned to her in an unfamiliar shape has lost something real, and the words she does not recognize stand for knowledge that was not passed on. But the complaint measures revival against the wrong standard. Every language that is spoken changes, and a language that does not change across a generation is usually one that is no longer spoken. The question that decides whether a revival has succeeded is not whether the children sound like their grandparents. It is whether they use the language when no adult is asking them to.

[6] By that standard the evidence is more mixed than the enrollment figures suggest. Teachers in a number of immersion programs have reported a familiar pattern: children answer in the heritage language in class and switch to English the moment they reach the playground. The language has become the school's language, something performed for adults, rather than the children's own. The sociolinguist Joshua Fishman argued in the early 1990s that schools on their own cannot secure a threatened language; unless it returns to homes and neighborhoods, a school can produce speakers without producing a speech community.

[7] That is why the most closely watched figures in Hawaiian and Māori revival are not test scores but births. Some of the children from the first nests are now parents, and a share of them are raising their own children in the language at home. Whatever those children's speech sounds like to their great-grandparents, it is being learned the way languages have always been learned, from infancy and from family. If revival has a finish line, it is the kitchen, the last place the language left.

passage_title: The Second Shooting
passage:
[1] Wren Halloway made nine documentary films between 1971 and 1996, and the one thing nearly every review of them said was that she was not in them. Her films had no narrator, no interviews, no music laid over the images, and no titles explaining who anyone was. A critic for one of the trade papers called her "the most invisible filmmaker working," and he meant it as praise. The phrase stuck. Festival programs repeated it, and so did the catalog of the retrospective mounted after her death. For twenty years audiences were told that a Halloway film showed you what happened when no one was directing it.

[2] That account is not exactly false, but it describes what she declined to do rather than what she did. Consider The Crossing, her film about a car ferry that worked a cold northern strait through one winter. Halloway and a single camera operator rode the ferry for four months and came back with roughly two hundred hours of footage. The finished film runs ninety-four minutes. Somewhere between those two figures lie more than a hundred and ninety hours of decisions, and every one of them is hers. A narrator tells you what to think in a sentence you can hear and dispute. A cut tells you what to think in a silence you never notice.

[3] Halloway understood this better than her admirers did. In a rare interview late in her life she called editing "the second shooting," and said that it was in the editing room, not on the deck, that her films found out what they were about. The economy of her cutting is famous: a scene ends the instant its point has landed, sometimes in the middle of a gesture, so that the viewer is pushed into the next scene before he has finished with the last. Less often noticed is the opposite habit. Near the middle of The Crossing she holds a single shot for nearly four minutes, a woman in a parked car waiting for the ferry to dock, doing nothing at all. No information arrives during those four minutes. What arrives is the length of the wait, which is the subject of the film.

[4] The clearest evidence against her supposed invisibility is a scene that a stricter observational filmmaker would have cut. A young deckhand, coiling rope, glances up, sees the camera, and simply looks into it for several seconds before turning back to his work. The shot breaks the convention that the people in a documentary do not notice they are being filmed. Halloway kept it, and when asked why, she said she would rather show the audience that she had been there than pretend she had not.

[5] Her obligations ran in another direction as well. Before releasing a film she screened it privately for the people in it. After one such screening, a ferry cook asked her to remove a scene in which he wept over a letter from his son. By the account of her editor, it was the strongest sequence in the film. She took it out and did not replace it, and the cut is still visible to an attentive viewer as a small jump in the light. Halloway never discussed the decision in public; the editor's account is the only one there is.

[6] None of this makes the old praise worthless. Halloway's restraint was real; she did not tell her audiences what to feel, and the absence of a voice gave her films a quiet that other documentaries of the period did not have. But restraint is a method, not an absence, and its effects are not innocent. A viewer who leaves The Crossing feeling that nobody told her what to think has in fact been told a great deal, only through arrangement rather than speech, and has been left free to believe that the conclusions were her own. That freedom is what makes the films moving. It is also what makes them worth watching twice, the second time with an eye on the cuts.

passage_title: What a Chewed Leaf Gives Away
passage:
[1] A plant cannot run from something that is eating it, and it has no teeth or claws with which to fight back. Unlike most animals, it can usually survive the loss of a good part of itself, but it cannot afford to lose too much. What it has to protect itself is chemistry. Leaves, stems, and roots produce an enormous range of compounds whose main purpose, as far as biologists can tell, is to make the plant unpleasant, indigestible, or poisonous to the animals that feed on it. Some of these compounds are present all the time. Many others are made only after an attack has begun, and the difference between the two strategies turns out to be largely a matter of cost.

[2] Defense is expensive. Nicotine, which wild tobacco plants produce in larger amounts after they are damaged, is built partly from nitrogen, and for a plant growing in poor soil nitrogen is dear: every molecule spent on poison is a molecule not spent on leaves, roots, or seeds. Experiments with many species have found that plants forced to keep their defenses switched on tend to grow more slowly than plants that are not. A defense manufactured only when needed avoids paying that price in seasons when nothing is eating the plant, at the risk of being late when something is.

[3] The speed and reach of these induced defenses surprised the researchers who first measured them. In a well-known study published in 1972, scientists who wounded a single leaf of a tomato plant found that compounds called proteinase inhibitors, which interfere with an insect's ability to digest protein, soon built up not only in the wounded leaf but in undamaged leaves elsewhere on the plant. Something was carrying the news. Later work identified a family of plant hormones, the jasmonates, as central to the signal.

[4] Some defenses do not act on the attacker directly at all. When caterpillars chew the leaves of a corn plant, the plant releases a blend of volatile compounds into the air, and parasitic wasps follow that scent to the caterpillars, in whose bodies they lay their eggs. The response is surprisingly specific. Leaves torn mechanically release a far weaker blend; the full response depends on compounds in the caterpillar's saliva. The plant, in other words, can distinguish being eaten from being merely damaged, and it summons help only for the first.

[5] Airborne compounds raised a more startling possibility. In the early 1980s, researchers reported that undamaged trees growing near damaged ones increased their own chemical defenses, and the popular press quickly announced that trees could warn one another. Other scientists pointed to weaknesses in the experiments, and for years the idea was treated with suspicion. Later field work, notably on sagebrush and wild tobacco, gave it firmer support: plants exposed to the air around clipped neighbors did, under some conditions, suffer less damage afterward.

[6] Whether "warning" is the right word is another matter. A plant gains nothing obvious by protecting a neighbor that competes with it for light and water. One explanation now taken seriously is that the airborne signal is mainly a message a plant sends to itself. Internal signals travel through the plant's vascular system, and that plumbing connects some leaves closely and others hardly at all, so that a branch on the far side of a stem may learn of an attack slowly or not at all. Air takes a shorter route. In one study of wild lima beans, leaves that were poorly connected to a damaged leaf nonetheless strengthened their defenses when exposed to its airborne compounds, and did not when that air was kept from them.

[7] If this explanation is right, the neighbors are not being warned. They are overhearing. A plant that detects the chemical distress of the plant beside it is reading a message that was never addressed to it, and that turns out to be useful anyway. The sharing, where it happens, may be less a kindness than an accident of chemistry that the listeners have learned to exploit.
